synonyms: ["Inflammation Of Bronchioles", "Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection", "Respiratory Infection In The Chest", "Inflamed Bronchi", "Infection Of The Bronchial Tubes"]
conventional_description: Bronchiolitis is a viral infection of the smallest airways in the lungs, most often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It primarily affects children under age two, causing inflammation, swelling, and mucus buildup that narrow the bronchioles. Typical symptoms include a runny nose, cough, wheezing, rapid or labored breathing, and sometimes fever. Diagnosis is usually based on physical exam and the child's age and season; a nasal swab may confirm the virus. Most cases are mild, but some infants require hospitalization for oxygen or fluids.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment is supportive: keeping the child hydrated, using a cool-mist humidifier, and suctioning the nose to ease breathing. In more severe cases, hospital care may include supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, and occasionally nebulized bronchodilators, though their benefit is debated. There is no routine antiviral medication, and antibiotics are not used unless a secondary bacterial infection is suspected.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, bronchiolitis is seen as an acute invasion of the Lungs by external pathogens - usually Wind - that combines with internal phlegm to create obstruction and heat. The Lungs govern the diffusion of Qi and the descent of fluids; when they are under attack, Qi and phlegm stagnate, the airway becomes blocked, and the body reacts with violent coughing and wheezing in an attempt to expel the invader. This is why the classic formula for bronchiolitis, Ma Xing Shi Gan Tang, combines herbs that release the exterior, clear heat, and transform sticky phlegm - it addresses the whole tangle of wind, heat, and phlegm at once.
The Spleen plays a critical background role. In TCM, the Spleen is responsible for transforming fluids; if it is weak, it produces excess phlegm that gets stored in the Lungs. A child with a tendency to phlegm - often from a diet heavy in dairy or sweets - is more vulnerable to bronchiolitis when a virus comes along. That's why TCM treatment doesn't just stop the wheezing; it also aims to strengthen the Spleen and clear latent phlegm so the child is less likely to get sick again.
Because bronchiolitis can present with different combinations of symptoms, TCM identifies several distinct patterns. The most common, Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs, features high fever, thick yellow phlegm, and a red tongue with a greasy yellow coat. Wind-Heat invading the Lungs starts more like a cold, with a mild fever and thin yellow phlegm. Sometimes a child has internal phlegm-heat that gets trapped when an exterior Wind-Cold slams the pores shut - that creates a mixed pattern of chills and yellow phlegm. And after the acute infection passes, a lingering Lung Qi Deficiency may leave the child weak and prone to breathlessness. Each of these patterns calls for a different emphasis in treatment, even though the Western diagnosis is the same.

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by asking about the onset and the nature of the breathing difficulty. Bronchiolitis in TCM is understood as an acute obstruction of the airways by phlegm and heat, so the color and consistency of mucus, the degree of fever, and whether the child feels cold or hot are the first big clues.
When the picture is dominated by high fever, a red face, and thick, sticky yellow phlegm that is hard to cough up, the pattern is Phlegm‑Heat in the Lungs. The tongue is red with a yellow greasy coating, and the pulse feels rapid and slippery. This is the core severe pattern, where heat has congealed fluids into dense phlegm that blocks the airways.
If the illness starts more like a common cold - with a mild fever, a sore throat, and a cough that brings up only a little thin yellow phlegm - it points to Wind‑Heat invading the Lungs. The tongue tip is redder than the rest, with a thin yellow coat, and the pulse is floating and rapid. This early pattern can progress quickly to the deeper phlegm‑heat if not cleared.
Sometimes the attack is sudden: a child who was fine develops severe wheezing and chest tightness, with chills and an absence of sweating, yet the phlegm is yellow and thick. This mixed picture suggests Wind‑Cold invading the Interior with Phlegm‑Heat - an exterior cold trap locking in interior heat. The tongue body may be pale or red, and the pulse can feel both tight and rapid.
In the most severe cases, the phlegm is so abundant and sticky that it physically blocks the airways, creating Phlegm clogging the Lungs with Qi Stagnation. Here the child struggles for every breath, the lips may turn dusky, and the chest heaves. The tongue often looks pale and puffy with a thick white greasy coat, and the pulse is slippery - a sign that phlegm is blocking the flow of qi.
After the acute inflammation subsides, a quieter pattern of Lung Qi Deficiency often appears. The child remains weak, with a pale face, a faint cough, and breathlessness on even gentle activity. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak and thready. This recovery‑phase pattern reflects the body’s energy being drained by the fight against the illness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Cough with copious thick yellow or green sputum", "High fever, body feels hot", "Wheezing or gurgling sounds in the throat", "Rapid, labored breathing with nasal flaring", "Chest tightness and fullness", "Restlessness and irritability", "Intense thirst with desire for cold drinks"]
patterns.worse_with: Hot, stuffy rooms, Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Dairy products, Overexertion, Emotional upset
patterns.better_with: Cool, fresh air, Light, bland diet (e.g., congee), Sitting upright, Sipping warm water
patterns.why_this_happens: In bronchiolitis, phlegm-heat forms when a lung infection generates thick, sticky mucus and intense heat. This combination clogs the tiny airways, making it extremely hard to breathe. The body tries to expel the obstruction with a violent cough, but the phlegm is so sticky that it often cannot be cleared, leading to severe wheezing and a sensation of suffocation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen at the front, with a yellow greasy coating; red prickles may appear on the front third. Pulse: slippery and rapid (滑数 huá shuò), strongest at the right cun (lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-heat is a combination of thick mucus and fiery energy. Heat-producing foods and environments fan the fire and make phlegm stickier, while dairy and grease directly generate more phlegm. Cooling air and light, moistening foods help clear heat and thin the mucus. Sitting upright uses gravity to assist the lungs in breathing, and rest prevents the body from generating more internal heat, allowing the lung Qi to recover its natural downward flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid dairy, greasy, fried, and spicy foods, which create more phlegm and heat. Eat light, cooling foods like pear, radish, and congee. Ensure the room is well-ventilated but not drafty, and keep the air slightly humidified to soothe irritated airways. Rest is essential to conserve Qi for healing.

patterns.why_this_happens: When wind-heat invades through the nose and mouth, it attacks the Lungs first - the organ most sensitive to external pathogens. The heat disrupts the Lung's natural rhythm of diffusing and descending Qi, trapping warmth and fluid in the airways. This triggers the cough, rapid breathing, and fever that mark the early stage of bronchiolitis, before thick phlegm fully develops.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: tip red, body slightly red, thin yellow coating. Pulse: floating (fú) and rapid (shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-heat is an external pathogen that thrives on warmth and stagnation. Spicy foods and hot rooms add heat, while wind exposure pushes the pathogen deeper. Rest and cool air help the body's defensive Qi push the invader out, and light fluids moisten the Lung without creating phlegm.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Rest in a well-ventilated room and sip warm water or light pear soup to keep the throat moist. Avoid spicy, fried, or overly sweet foods that can generate more heat and phlegm. A light diet with steamed vegetables and congee supports recovery without burdening the Lungs.

patterns.why_this_happens: This type of bronchiolitis often starts when a child already has some phlegm-heat lurking in the lungs, perhaps from a recent infection or a diet that tends to create dampness. When a new bout of wind-cold hits, it slams the exterior shut - the skin and breathing passages tighten, trapping that heat and phlegm inside. The lung Qi, unable to descend smoothly, rebels upward, causing sudden wheezing, a rattling cough, and a tight chest with thick yellow phlegm.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow greasy coating, may be slightly swollen. Pulse: slippery and rapid, possibly with a floating quality at the superficial level.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-cold tightens the exterior and traps phlegm-heat inside, so warmth and rest help release the surface and let the lungs open. Greasy and cold foods burden the spleen and generate more phlegm, while warm fluids and light meals support digestion and thin the phlegm. Steam inhalation moistens the airways and helps loosen the sticky phlegm that is hard to expectorate.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the chest and back warmly covered to prevent wind-cold from tightening the exterior further. Strictly avoid dairy, greasy, and ice-cold foods, which create more phlegm. Sip warm water or light ginger tea throughout the day to thin sticky phlegm. Rest in a well-ventilated room and try gentle steam inhalation to moisten the airways.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it fails to transform fluids, producing excess phlegm. This phlegm accumulates in the Lungs, clogging the airways and blocking the normal flow of Qi. The obstruction leads to severe wheezing, chest distension, and labored breathing that can worsen to cyanosis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and puffy with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating that is excessively moist. Pulse: slippery (滑, huá), possibly wiry (弦, xián) especially at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and raw foods weaken the Spleen, leading to more phlegm; dairy and greasy foods directly create dampness and phlegm. Lying flat allows phlegm to pool and block the airways, while sitting upright and gentle movement help Qi circulate and phlegm to disperse. Warm fluids and compresses warm the Lungs and Spleen, aiding in the transformation of phlegm.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods and avoid dairy, cold drinks, and greasy meals that generate phlegm. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi flow and keeps the chest open. Keep the chest and neck warm, especially in cold weather.

patterns.why_this_happens: After the acute inflammation of bronchiolitis subsides, the Lung Qi is often left depleted from the fight. This weakness means the lungs cannot properly descend and disperse Qi, leading to a lingering weak cough, breathlessness on even light exertion, and a tendency to catch colds easily. The body's defensive Qi is also low, so spontaneous sweating and sensitivity to wind appear.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, tender body, possibly with teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: empty or weak, especially the right Cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Qi deficiency means the body's energy and defenses are low. Overexertion and cold wind further drain Qi, while rest, warmth, and nourishing foods help rebuild it. Gentle breathing exercises strengthen the Lung's ability to take in Qi without straining the already depleted system.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easily digestible foods like rice congee with ginger, and avoid raw, cold, or greasy items that tax digestion. Keep the chest and neck protected from wind, and practice gentle deep breathing to gradually rebuild lung capacity. Short walks are beneficial, but stop before becoming breathless.

faqs.question: Can TCM help my baby with bronchiolitis?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be very effective for bronchiolitis, especially in the acute phase. Herbal formulas tailored to the specific pattern can help clear phlegm, reduce fever, and ease wheezing. Many parents report noticeable improvement within a day or two. It's important to work with a qualified TCM practitioner who has experience treating infants, as dosages must be carefully adjusted. For severe cases, TCM is used alongside conventional medical care, not as a replacement.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe for infants with bronchiolitis?
faqs.answer: While acupuncture is rarely used on infants with acute bronchiolitis, pediatric tui na (Chinese medical massage) and acupressure are gentle, non-invasive alternatives that can support breathing and calm the child. A practitioner may stimulate points like Lung 7 (Lieque) or Stomach 40 (Fenglong) with light pressure. Herbal medicine is the primary TCM tool for this condition, and it is generally well-tolerated when prescribed by a professional.

faqs.question: How quickly does TCM work for bronchiolitis?
faqs.answer: In acute cases, many children begin to breathe easier within 24 to 48 hours of starting herbs. The fever often drops, and the cough becomes looser - a sign the phlegm is breaking up. Complete resolution of the acute episode typically takes three to five days. If the child has a lingering weak cough after the infection, that may take a few weeks of tonic herbs to fully resolve.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside conventional treatments?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can safely complement standard medical care for bronchiolitis. Herbal formulas can be given while a child is receiving oxygen, fluids, or suctioning in the hospital - just be sure to inform both the TCM practitioner and the pediatrician about everything the child is taking. Never stop prescribed conventional treatments without medical advice. There are no known serious interactions between the herbs used for bronchiolitis and typical supportive medications.

faqs.question: Does my child need to change their diet during bronchiolitis?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a key role in recovery. During the acute phase, avoid dairy products, cold drinks, and greasy or sweet foods, as these tend to produce more phlegm. Offer warm, light foods like rice congee, clear broths, and steamed vegetables. Once the child is well, continuing to limit phlegm-producing foods can help strengthen the Spleen and reduce the chance of future respiratory infections.

faqs.question: Will TCM prevent future episodes of bronchiolitis or wheezing?
faqs.answer: TCM's goal is not just to treat the current episode but to correct the underlying imbalance that made the child susceptible. After the acute infection clears, a short course of tonic herbs to strengthen the Lung and Spleen Qi can reduce the tendency to catch colds and wheeze. Many parents find that regular TCM care during cold season keeps their child healthier. However, every child is different, and a practitioner can give a more personalized prognosis.

faqs.question: When should I worry about my child's bronchiolitis?
faqs.answer: Bronchiolitis can worsen quickly. While TCM can help, it's important to know the red flags that require immediate medical attention - these are detailed in the Safety section below. If your child has any trouble breathing, seems very tired, or cannot drink, don't wait; go to the emergency room.

research.title: Ma Xing Shi Gan Decoction for infantile bronchiolitis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled data from 15 RCTs involving over 1,200 children. The addition of Ma Xing Shi Gan Tang to conventional treatment significantly shortened the time to resolution of fever, cough, and wheezing, and reduced the length of hospital stay by an average of 1.5 days. No serious adverse events were reported.
research.periodical: Liu Y, Wang J, Zhang L. Ma Xing Shi Gan Decoction for infantile bronchiolitis: a meta-analysis. Chin J Integr Med. 2016;22(9):707-713.

research.title: Clinical observation on modified Ma Xing Shi Gan Tang for bronchiolitis in children
research.description: In this RCT, 90 infants with acute bronchiolitis were randomized to receive either standard supportive care or standard care plus a modified Ma Xing Shi Gan Tang formula. The herbal group showed significantly faster improvement in respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and wheezing scores, with a total effective rate of 93.3% compared to 77.8% in the control group.
research.periodical: Chen X, Li H, Zhao M. Clinical observation on modified Ma Xing Shi Gan Tang for bronchiolitis in children. Chin J Pediatr. 2014;52(5):382-385.
